sections.text: You built an app. Your friends love it. Does that mean customers will pay? Not yet—you have evidence of interest, but not of paying demand.

sections.text: A business provides something customers value in exchange for payment. To understand how it works, start with three parts: customer, offer, and delivery.

sections.text: The customer is the person or organization buying. Ask: who are they, and what do they need?

sentences.text: The customer is the person or organization buying.

sections.text: The offer is what they can buy: a clear product or service, its price, and what is included.

sections.text: Delivery is how they receive what you promised. Payment can happen before or after delivery, depending on the arrangement.

sections.text: For example, Maya sells a seventy-nine-dollar invoicing guide to freelance designers.

sections.text: Her customers are freelance designers who need help organizing invoices. Her offer is the guide for seventy-nine dollars. She delivers it through a download link.

sections.text: Now compare that with an app that friends praise but nobody buys. The feedback may be useful. It does not yet show that customers will pay. A purchase gives stronger evidence of paying demand, although one sale does not prove long-term success.
